source.citation: John Ford Barbour, article on cerebro-spinal concussion, Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease 18 (1891): 147–148. Title to confirm from the page image.

complaints: pain in the abdominal muscles, worse after eating and in damp weather
weak and tired; walks like an old man
low spirits; loss of business ability
presentation.course: Struck in the stomach by an air-brake handle in a railway accident in September 1888; off work six months. In February 1890 thrown through the cab window in a collision and pinned for four hours; broken fibula. Has lost 24 pounds since.

findings: pupils dilated and unequal; the left reacts only slightly to light
slow, slurred speech that drops the ends of words

treatments.treatment: sulfonal, with local and general electrization, for about three months
treatments.response: gained five pounds, sleeps without a hypnotic, walks more briskly, able to do light work

outcome: Improved; able to pursue a light occupation.
quotes: Being born under an unlucky star, he was in a collision

modernReading.text: Uncertain. The author reads it as injury to the nervous system. Unequal, sluggish pupils, a failing knee reflex, slurred speech, and a change in character would also raise general paresis (late syphilis) or a head injury. His improvement argues somewhat against paresis.

fixed: weight loss, poor sleep, weakness, low spirits
unequal pupils and one weak knee reflex

constrained.rule: railway work: engineer, fireman, brakeman, conductor; or a passenger

notes: The same article describes engine-drivers woken by an electric gong and a woman awarded $10,000 damages. Litigation is a natural complication for a procedural version.
